title: Gbegiri
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: Peeled beans cooked to collapse with no salt at all, mashed with the ijabe or blended, then pushed through a sieve — the second de-skinning that most people skip.
longDesc: Gbegiri is the yellow bean half of abula, and the whole dish is about getting the skins out. They come off twice: once from the soaked raw bean, by hand or by pulsing it in a blender until each bean splits, and again after cooking, when the puree goes through a sieve and the chaff is discarded. Salt is withheld until the beans are soft, which the author says makes them cook faster. It thickens very fast once it is done, so expect to loosen it.
ingredients: 2 cups water to start, more as needed
steps: Soak the beans, then peel — by hand, or pulse a few times in a jug blender so each bean splits and the skin falls off, and finish by hand.
Cook the peeled beans with water, starting with 2 cups and adding more as needed, until very soft and mushy. Do not add salt at this stage.
Mash with an ijabe or a whisk; or cool slightly and blend smooth with about half a cup of water.
If you mashed by hand, pass the puree through a sieve to remove the clumps.
Return it to low heat and add water to a semi-fluid consistency.
Add the palm oil, iru, crayfish powder, bouillon cube, ground pepper and salt.
Cook 5 to 7 minutes, stirring, until it has thickened and the palm oil is well combined.
chefTips: No salt until the beans are soft. Salt early and they take much longer.
Pulse, do not blend, to peel. You want each bean to split, not to puree raw beans.
The sieve is the step people drop, and it is the difference between velvet and grit. Push it through and throw the chaff away.
The palm oil is not bleached for gbegiri. No gbegiri source consulted bleaches it — that is an ayamase technique, not a general palm-oil step.
It thickens quickly and will keep thickening as it cools. The author's own note: do not be alarmed, just add a bit of water and reheat.
Done is when it has thickened and the oil has stopped sitting separate on top.
Unpeeled beans will work at a push — one named source says so outright — but you will not get the smooth yellow texture the dish is known for.
commonMistakes: Salting the beans at the start.
Blending the raw soaked beans instead of pulsing them.
Judging the consistency hot — it will be much thicker cold.
sources: Adapted from 'Gbegiri Soup Recipe', byline Sisi Jemimah — 2 cups black-eyed or brown beans, 3 tablespoons palm oil, 2 tablespoons crayfish powder, 1 tablespoon locust beans, 1 to 2 tablespoons ground dried pepper, 1 Knorr cube, salt to taste; start the cooking water at 2 cups; blend with about half a cup of water; cook 5 to 7 minutes at the end. The no-salt instruction, the ijabe-or-whisk mash, the sieve step and the thickens-quickly note are all hers.

Her peeling method, as printed: 'soak the beans for 10 minutes then, using the pulse function on your jug blender, pulse a few times. This will cause each bean to split and the skin to fall off. Then pour in a bowl and complete peeling by hand.' The 10 minutes is from her moin moin page; the gbegiri page says only 'soak then peel'.

DISAGREEMENT on whether the skins must come off, not reconciled. Sisi Jemimah and Tribune Online's Testimony Ishola both peel. Ajoke at My Active Kitchen peels but states unpeeled beans are acceptable (NGA005). Abi Olayiwola skips peeling entirely by starting from canned beans and flags that as her own shortcut (NGA119).
DISAGREEMENT on sieving: always (Tribune, Ajoke), only if hand-mashed (Sisi Jemimah), or never (Abi Olayiwola).

On the palm oil: Ajoke is explicit that it is heated about 3 minutes 'without bleaching oil'. No gbegiri source consulted bleaches, which is worth recording against the ayamase recipes (NGA016, NGA017, NGA018) where bleaching is the defining step.
reheating: Low heat with water to loosen. It sets firm when cold.
healthBenefits: Cowpeas are high in plant protein, folate and soluble fibre.
Red palm oil carries vitamin E and carotenoids.
culturalNote: Gbegiri is buka food — the roadside eating houses of the southwest, where it arrives beside ewedu with a ladle of stew over both. The same bean soup turns up in the north as miyan wake, which 9jafoodie glosses directly as gbegiri, making it one of the few dishes with a settled name on both sides of the country.
